metadata.title: HPSC FSO — Food Processing Operations & Commodity Technology: 100-Question Practice Bank
metadata.source_scope: Uploaded 68-page handout: dairy; cereals, pulses and grain technology; meat, poultry, fish and egg; horticultural processing.
metadata.option_format: Four-option MCQs (A–D); an integrated three-statement count item is included.
metadata.exam_alignment_note: This is a source-grounded MCQ practice bank for objective recall and concept checking. The current HPSC 2026 Subject Knowledge Test is reported as subjective/descriptive; MCQs do not reproduce that paper format. Use the explanations to convert mechanisms and process sequences into descriptive answers.
metadata.source_caveat: Numbers marked as conventions in the handout may vary by textbook. Regulatory/grading values must be checked against currently notified FSSR/BIS/USDA text before being quoted as law. The handout includes a correction/qualification register; illustrative textbook values are not treated as universal statutory limits.
metadata.source_method: Questions drafted from the uploaded handout's explanatory text, tables, HPSC EXAM TRAP callouts, correction register, revision bank and model-answer sections.

questions.unit: Unit 5: Food Processing Operations & Commodity Technology
questions.question: A fresh commodity weighs 10 kg and yields 2 kg after dehydration. Its dehydration ratio is:

detailed_explanations.explanation: Added water moves milk's freezing point towards 0 °C. Cryoscopy is preferred because added solutes may mask a fall in specific gravity, whereas cryoscopy responds to dissolved solutes. It detects added water, not skimming.

The freezing point has moved towards zero, the expected direction when water dilutes lactose and salts. A single result is an adulteration indicator and should be interpreted using the laboratory reference and method.
Milk is polyphasic: fat globules form an oil-in-water emulsion, casein micelles form a colloidal suspension, and lactose, soluble minerals and other small solutes are in true solution.
The handout gives casein as about 80% of milk protein; whey proteins account for most of the remainder.
Stokes' velocity is proportional to the square of particle diameter. Doubling diameter therefore increases velocity fourfold, all other factors unchanged.
Warm milk has lower viscosity and the fat is fully liquid, improving centrifugal separation. This is a unit-operation condition, not a sterilisation step.
The closely spaced discs (about 0.4–0.6 mm apart in the handout) shorten the separation path and increase efficiency.

Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Cryoscopy is a reference test for added water; skimming changes fat and specific gravity, not the freezing-point signal in the same diagnostic way. Simultaneous changes can mask lactometer readings.
The first stage reduces globule size. The second stage breaks up clusters formed when newly created globules stick together through shared protein coatings.
Homogenisation disrupts the native milk-fat-globule membrane and exposes lipid surfaces, making lipolysis more likely. It is not a microbial kill step and is commonly paired with pasteurisation.
LTLT/holder pasteurisation is 63 °C for 30 minutes. The 72 °C for 15 seconds condition is HTST.
HTST uses approximately 72 °C for 15 seconds (the handout notes 71.7 °C for 15 seconds in Indian practice).
Native milk alkaline phosphatase is slightly more heat resistant than the target pasteurisation pathogen. A negative result supports adequate pasteurisation; it does not prove sterilisation.

In the turbidity test, whey proteins in raw/pasteurised milk precipitate after filtration and boiling. In adequately sterilised/UHT milk they are denatured and removed during filtration, leaving a clear filtrate.
ALP is inactivated by pasteurisation, while lactoperoxidase survives HTST and is destroyed above about 80 °C. The pattern helps distinguish pasteurisation from excessive heating.
Ultrafiltration retains proteins (casein and whey) and fat, while lactose, minerals, water and non-protein nitrogen largely pass into permeate.
RO uses a dense membrane and high pressure; it retains essentially all solutes and allows water to pass, concentrating the milk or whey.
During the constant-rate period, free water evaporates from a saturated surface and the rate is governed mainly by air conditions. Internal diffusion dominates the falling-rate period.
Spray-dried lactose is amorphous. Water acts as a plasticiser, lowering Tg; above the sticky-point region particles adhere to one another and to dryer walls.
Cream is an oil-in-water emulsion. Churning destabilises fat globules and causes coalescence, producing butter as a water-in-oil emulsion.
The handout lists table butter milk fat not less than 80%, moisture not more than 16%, curd not more than 1.5%, and salt not more than 3%.
Milk fat is rich in short-chain water-soluble volatile fatty acids, giving a high RM value. Vegetable oils generally lower RM and raise the butyro-refractometer reading.
Polenske value reflects water-insoluble volatile fatty acids such as caprylic, capric and lauric acids. Coconut and palm-kernel oils can raise it markedly.
Milk is heated, cooled to the coagulation range and acidified. The handout stresses pH 5.3–5.4 as more important than memorising a single coagulation temperature.
Dhap khoa has the highest moisture (about 35–40%) and a loose, sticky body; it is suitable for gulab jamun and pantua.
The handout gives husk at about 20–22% of paddy, bran at 5–10%, germ at 2–3%, and endosperm around 70%.
Oppositely rotating rubber rolls with a speed differential shear the husk off while minimising kernel breakage. The unshelled paddy is separated and returned.
The handout identifies about 13–14% moisture as suitable for milling. Excessive or insufficient moisture and fissures increase breakage.
The handout defines head rice as whole kernels at least three-quarters the length of an intact kernel. It is a key economic milling index.
Parboiling is a hydrothermal treatment of paddy before milling. The husk remains during soaking and steaming, allowing soluble nutrients to migrate inward.
The standard sequence is cleaning/soaking, steaming to gelatinise starch, drying to safe milling moisture, then milling.
Starch gelatinises during steaming and re-solidifies on drying into a hard, more continuous mass. Fissures are sealed and the kernel resists breakage during milling.
Water-soluble nutrients including thiamine and niacin diffuse inward during soaking/steaming. This increases their retention in milled parboiled rice compared with raw milled rice.
The handout gives bran about 14–15%, endosperm about 83%, and germ 2–3%. The starchy endosperm is the principal flour fraction.
Added water plasticises and toughens the bran so it comes off in larger flakes, while weakening the bran-endosperm bond and making endosperm easier to reduce.
Break rolls are corrugated/fluted and use a higher speed differential (about 2.5:1) to shear open the kernel and scrape endosperm from bran.
Reduction rolls are smooth and use a lower differential to crush purified semolina and middlings into flour with minimal bran fragmentation.
Purifiers combine an inclined oscillating sieve with controlled aspiration. Lighter bran is lifted while denser endosperm particles pass through, reducing flour ash.
Atta retains most of the kernel, giving an extraction rate around 95–100%. Maida is much lower, around 70–72%, and patent flour around 40–60%.
The handout describes steeping with sulphur dioxide to condition kernels and facilitate separation of germ, fibre, starch and gluten. Lime-based nixtamalisation is a different process.
The germ is less dense and floats in hydrocyclones. Starch and gluten are subsequently separated using density differences, commonly centrifugation.
The handout identifies gluten as lighter than starch; centrifugation separates the lighter gluten fraction from the denser starch fraction.
A small oil application is a conditioning aid that helps loosen the husk. It is not a frying/flavouring operation and does not replace moist-heat cooking.
The seed coat contributes fibre and tannins, so dehulling can reduce these. Flatulence-causing oligosaccharides are largely in the cotyledon and are not removed simply by dehulling.
The handout distinguishes dry-milling conditioning from cooking. Moist heat is important for inactivating heat-labile trypsin inhibitors; dry-milling oil/heat is not a substitute.
Much of rice thiamine is concentrated in bran and germ. Greater bran removal improves whiteness but reduces thiamine and lipid content.
Dehusking removes the inedible husk to produce brown rice. Whitening/polishing then removes bran and much of the germ to produce white rice.
Excess water can make the mill choke and create storage/mould problems. Under-conditioning causes bran fragmentation and higher ash contamination.
Hard wheat varieties generally produce stronger gluten-forming protein networks, supporting gas retention and bread structure.
The starchy endosperm is separated and reduced into flour. Bran and germ are distinct fractions with higher fibre, minerals or lipid content.
A sarcomere is the repeating unit of a myofibril bounded by Z-lines and containing overlapping thick (myosin) and thin (actin) filaments.
Oxymyoglobin contains ferrous iron bound to oxygen and gives the bright cherry-red colour. Deoxymyoglobin is purplish-red; metmyoglobin is brown.
With no circulation or oxygen delivery, muscle uses stored glycogen through anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactic acid and a limited amount of ATP.
Anaerobic glycolysis converts glycogen-derived intermediates to pyruvate and lactate. Lactic acid accumulates because blood circulation no longer removes metabolites.
ATP is required for myosin heads to detach from actin. When ATP becomes depleted, cross-bridges remain locked and muscle stiffens.
ATP is not restored post-mortem to release the original actomyosin cross-bridges. Endogenous proteases weaken the cytoskeletal/myofibrillar framework, tenderising the meat.
Calpains are calcium-activated neutral proteases and act early after slaughter. Cathepsins are lysosomal acid proteases that contribute as pH falls.
PSE means pale, soft, exudative. Acute stress causes rapid glycolysis and pH fall while carcass temperature remains high, denaturing proteins and reducing water-holding capacity.
DFD means dark, firm, dry. Chronic stress depletes glycogen before slaughter, so less lactic acid forms and ultimate pH remains high; the meat retains water but has poor microbial keeping quality.
DFD meat has high ultimate pH, which favours microbial growth and shortens shelf life. PSE has low pH and poor water-holding capacity.
Nitrite-derived nitric oxide reacts with myoglobin to form nitrosomyoglobin; heating produces the stable pink nitrosohaemochrome pigment.

Nitrite can react with secondary amines under favourable conditions, particularly high-temperature cooking, to form N-nitrosamines. The handout notes control through limiting ingoing nitrite, ascorbate and avoiding overcooking.
Cold smoking is a low-temperature surface treatment, often over days. It does not cook the product and does not by itself ensure safety.
Smoke deposits phenolic, carbonyl and other compounds that contribute flavour, colour and some preservation. It is not a sterilisation step; softwoods with resins are generally avoided.
Fish muscle has limited glycogen, so ultimate pH remains relatively high (about 6.2–6.8), and psychrotrophic Gram-negative bacteria and endogenous enzymes promote rapid spoilage.
IMP is a nucleotide breakdown intermediate responsible for pleasant fresh-fish umami. Inosine is flavourless and hypoxanthine is bitter and associated with deterioration.
K-value is based on ATP breakdown products and increases as fish loses freshness. It is an early freshness index, unlike TVB-N/TMA-N which rise later in spoilage.
Certain bacteria reduce TMAO, a natural osmolyte in marine fish, to trimethylamine, which contributes to fishy odour. This pathway is not relevant in the same way to freshwater fish.
Histamine is heat-stable; cooking may kill bacteria but does not reliably destroy preformed histamine. Prevention depends on rapid chilling and temperature control.
The Haugh unit combines thick albumen height and egg weight, allowing comparison of interior quality among eggs of different sizes.
The handout gives AA as 72 and above, A as 60–71 and B as 31–59. Below 30 is considered unfit in the cited grading scheme.
Loss of carbon dioxide through shell pores shifts the albumen chemistry towards alkalinity; pH can rise from about 7.6 to 9.0–9.5.
Albumen thins and the yolk absorbs water, enlarges and flattens. Consequently both Haugh unit and yolk index decline, while the air cell enlarges due to water loss.
The handout's exam trap pairs green rot with Pseudomonas and black rot with Proteus; these organism-defect associations are easily reversed in objective questions.
Trans-ovarian contamination can place Salmonella Enteritidis inside the egg before shell formation. An intact-looking egg can therefore still present a food-safety hazard.
Harvested produce remains living tissue. It continues respiration, transpiration, ripening and senescence while using stored reserves.
RQ is CO2 evolved divided by O2 consumed. Carbohydrate oxidation gives an RQ near 1; lipid oxidation generally gives a value below 1.
Q10 is the ratio of reaction/respiration rate at T+10 °C to that at T. A value of 2–3 means the rate doubles or triples with a 10 °C rise in the stated range.

Tropical/subtropical commodities such as banana, mango, tomato and cucumber can suffer membrane-related chilling injury at low non-freezing temperatures. Each commodity has a minimum safe storage temperature.
The handout notes that a 5–10% loss of fresh weight can produce visible wilting, shrivelling and loss of crispness. High relative humidity and low temperature reduce transpiration.
Banana is climacteric and shows a respiration rise associated with ripening. Grape, citrus and pineapple are listed as non-climacteric examples.
Ethylene can influence respiration and some ripening responses in non-climacteric fruit, but it does not transform the fruit into a climacteric type.
The pathway is methionine → SAM → ACC → ethylene. ACC synthase catalyses the rate-limiting SAM-to-ACC step; ACC oxidase converts ACC to ethylene and requires oxygen.
Ripening apples release ethylene. Ethylene-sensitive leafy vegetables may yellow and senesce more rapidly, so mixed storage requires attention to ethylene compatibility.
Lower O2 and elevated CO2 can suppress respiration, ethylene action, softening and decay. CA/MAP complements refrigeration and is not a substitute for it.
Clostridium botulinum cannot grow at pH 4.6 or below under the conditions described. Low-acid foods above pH 4.6 require a more severe validated process.
The thermal process is designed around the most heat-resistant pathogen capable of growth in the product. For low-acid, anaerobically stored canned foods, C. botulinum spores are the key hazard.
Exhausting removes air from the can headspace and tissue before sealing. Subsequent cooling contracts the contents and creates the vacuum; retorting is the sterilising heat process.
Retorting applies a validated heat process to the sealed container to achieve the required microbial lethality. Exhausting, not retorting, is the operation associated with vacuum formation.
The handout identifies C-enamel for sulphur-rich foods, which can react with tin/iron and cause dark sulphide staining. R-enamel is associated with acid, coloured fruits.
Prompt cooling arrests cooking and prevents quality damage. The cited endpoint leaves enough residual heat to dry the can surface and reduce rusting.
Freezing reduces available liquid water and slows microbial and chemical activity, but it does not sterilise. Many microorganisms survive and enzymes may remain partly active.
Fast passage through the critical freezing zone favours many small crystals, reducing cellular damage and drip loss compared with slow freezing.
In dry freezer air, ice can sublime from an exposed product surface, leaving a dry, pale, spongy area. Vapour-tight packaging and glazing help prevent it.
The handout gives aw below about 0.6 as the level at which microbial growth stops. Enzymatic and non-enzymatic reactions may still occur at higher aw values.
Once the surface is no longer saturated, water must migrate from the interior. Product thickness, structure and temperature influence internal diffusion, and most drying time is spent in this period.
Very hot, dry initial air can dry and shrink the surface into a dense, poorly permeable skin while the centre remains wet. This slows further drying and can cause later spoilage.
In freeze-drying, the product is frozen and ice is removed directly as vapour under reduced pressure, bypassing the liquid phase.

Vegetables are commonly blanched before freezing or drying to inactivate quality-degrading enzymes. Fruits are often treated differently, for example with sulphuring or sugar rather than routine blanching.
Dehydration ratio = fresh weight/dried weight = 10/2 = 5. A higher ratio indicates more water was removed relative to the dried mass.
